fact.detail: South Dakota's 1957 act (S.D. Codified Laws §§ 1-1-12 to 1-1-16) offered to assume civil and criminal jurisdiction if the affected tribes consented; the Eighth Circuit found consent was not given, so jurisdiction was never assumed under it. (Rosebud Sioux Tribe v. South Dakota, 900 F.2d 1164, 1166 (8th Cir. 1990).)
fact.note: Section 1-1-13 says a tribe that took no action within one year of Oct. 1, 1957 is deemed to consent; the court nevertheless held consent was not given. The sections are still printed in the code. The related 1959 highway statute (§ 1-1-17) also never took effect because its condition (roads jointly maintained by State and United States) was never met (900 F.2d at 1166). Shakopee, Northern Cheyenne and Turtle Mountain have only trust-land presence in SD in the roster and are not mapped. Also cites: south-dakota-codified-laws-1-1-12, south-dakota-codified-laws-1-1-13.

fact.note: Quote is from Rosebud. A 1963 attempt to assume full jurisdiction (1963 S.D. Laws ch. 467) was defeated 3 to 1 in a referendum (900 F.2d at 1167). Codified Laws §§ 1-1-18 to 1-1-21) declared a general assumption of jurisdiction in Indian country, but it takes effect only on a gubernatorial proclamation, which was never issued; the general assumption never occurred. (S.D. Codified Laws § 1-1-21; 900 F.2d at 1167.)
fact.locator: S.D. Codified Laws § 1-1-21 (SL 1961, ch. 464, § 4); 900 F.2d at 1167
fact.note: Quote is from Rosebud. A 1963 attempt to assume full jurisdiction (1963 S.D. Laws ch. 467) was defeated 3 to 1 in a referendum (900 F.2d at 1167). fact.detail: South Dakota's 1961 highway-only assumption was held invalid by the South Dakota Supreme Court in 1964 (In re Hankins) and, after that court revived it in State v. Onihan (1988), by the Eighth Circuit in 1990: without tribal consent the State has no civil or criminal jurisdiction over highways through Indian lands. (Rosebud, 900 F.2d at 1166-67, 1172.)
fact.note: Hankins: 80 S.D. 435, 442-43, 125 N.W.2d 839, 842-43 (state cannot assume jurisdiction over highways alone; the Eighth Circuit describes this at 900 F.2d at 1167). Rosebud's further holding (at 1170-72): the highway-only scheme does not meet Public Law 280, and the 1968 consent requirement bars later nonconsensual assumption. Cert. history not checked. Parties: Rosebud, Cheyenne River, Oglala, Standing Rock; the holding is about "Indian lands in the state" generally. Also cites: in-re-hankins-petition-1964.

fact.detail: Today South Dakota holds no Public Law 280 jurisdiction over any of its reservations: the 1957 act was never consented to, the 1961 general act never took effect, and the 1961 highway piece is invalid; the statutes stay in the code. (Rosebud, 900 F.2d at 1166-67; S.D. Codified Laws §§ 1-1-12 to 1-1-21.)
fact.note: Quote is the 1957 assumption text, § 1-1-12, shown because it is still printed in the code. Conclusion that nothing is in force is mine, drawn from Rosebud (1990) plus the statutes; the research did not find any later tribal consent election or any post-1990 South Dakota assumption. Goldberg (2010) fn. 4 reaches the same view. Also cites: south-dakota-codified-laws-1-1-12, south-dakota-codified-laws-1-1-18.

fact.detail: The Supreme Court recorded that the Three Affiliated Tribes had not consented to state-court jurisdiction over Fort Berthold under ch. 27-19, so North Dakota had not assumed civil jurisdiction there. (Three Affiliated Tribes v. Wold Eng'g, 467 U.S. 138, 145 (1984).)
fact.note: Wold II (476 U.S. 877, 881) repeats the point; Wold II held ch. 27-19 pre-empted insofar as it disclaims pre-existing state jurisdiction over a tribe's suit against a non-Indian with no other forum, absent waiver of immunity. Wold the research dissent (Rehnquist, J., 467 U.S. at 162) says "North Dakota has not assumed any additional jurisdiction over Indian country under Pub. L. 280." Also cites: three-affiliated-tribes-v-wold-engineering-1986.

fact.detail: A 1946 act conferred on North Dakota jurisdiction over offenses by or against Indians on the Devils Lake (now Spirit Lake) Reservation to the same extent as elsewhere in the State, without ousting federal courts. (Act of May 31, 1946, ch. 279, 60 Stat. 229.)
fact.note: Criminal only. The Senate report (S. Rep. 116-130 at 2) identifies the Devils Lake Reservation as the Spirit Lake Reservation. Not codified in the U.S. Code. Also cites: senate-report-116-130.

fact.detail: Congress has not repealed the 1946 act. Repeal bills in the 115th (S. 2788) and 116th (S. 2159, H.R. 3831) Congresses were reported by the Senate committee or referred, and not enacted; the research found no public law repealing it through the 119th Congress listing. (S. Rep. No. 116-130, at 2 (2019).)
fact.note: "Not repealed" rests on absence: the Congress.gov API list of enacted laws for the 116th-119th Congresses (checked 2026-11-23; 119th list showed 144 laws) contains no repeal; govinfo BILLSTATUS for S. 2159 ends 2019-10-16 (placed on calendar) and for H.R. 3831 at 2019-08-02 (committee referral). The research did not find a 117th-119th Congress repeal bill. Verify before publishing. Also cites: statutes-at-large-60-229.

fact.detail: The Supreme Court held that Montana never took the "affirmative legislative action" needed to assume jurisdiction over the Blackfeet Reservation, so a tribal-council act could not give the State civil jurisdiction. (Kennerly v. Dist. Ct. of Mont., 400 U.S. 423, 425, 427 (1971).)
fact.note: Quote as printed in the official report (dash punctuation as in the PDF text). Holding at 427: the Tribal Council's unilateral action was insufficient under the 1953 Act.

fact.detail: Montana law lets any other tribe request state jurisdiction by resolution to the governor, who must proclaim it within 60 days, but only after the tribe's own approval and the consent of each affected county commission. (Mont. Code Ann. § 2-1-302.)
fact.note: Procedure only; the research found no proclamation under it for any other tribe. Under § 2-1-303 the State assumes jurisdiction 60 days after the proclamation. Enacted as 1963 Mont. Laws ch. 81 (section history lines).

fact.detail: The Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act subjects the Passamaquoddy Tribe and Penobscot Nation, their members and lands to Maine's jurisdiction as provided in the Maine Implementing Act, which applies state law and state court jurisdiction to them "except as otherwise provided." (Pub. L. No. 96-420, § 6(b)(1), 94 Stat. at 1794; Me. Rev. Stat. Ann. tit. 30, § 6204.)
fact.note: The Implementing Act also gives these two nations separate tribal jurisdiction in listed areas (30 M.R.S. §§ 6206, 6209-A, 6209-B; § 6(f) of the federal Act); the research read the federal grant and § 6204 only. § 6(c) removes federal criminal jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1152-1153 etc. Maine's 2022-2023 tribal-state legislation was not analyzed. 25 U.S.C. § 1725 is "omitted" from the Code and is cited here as the Statutes at Large section. Also cites: maine-revised-statutes-title-30-section-6204.

fact.detail: Indians and tribes in Maine other than the Passamaquoddy and Penobscot, including the Houlton Band of Maliseets, and their lands are subject to state civil and criminal jurisdiction and state courts as any other person or land, except where the Act provides otherwise. (Pub. L. No. 96-420, § 6(a), 94 Stat. at 1793.)
fact.note: Section 6(e)(2) (94 Stat. at 1794) lets the State and the Band agree on state jurisdiction over Band lands. Section 6(a) is "except as provided in section 8(e) and section 5(d)(4)." Houlton Band is not named in 6(a); it falls in "all other Indians." Section 6(b)(1) names only the two tribes.

fact.detail: Congress treated the Aroostook Band of Micmacs (now Mi'kmaq Nation) like the other Maine tribes under the 1980 settlement act and authorized Maine and the Band to agree on state jurisdiction over Band lands; Maine's 2023 Mi'kmaq Nation Restoration Act gives the Nation exclusive jurisdiction over listed matters. (Pub. L. No. 102-171, § 6(b), (d), 105 Stat. at 1148; Me. Rev. Stat. Ann. tit. 30, § 7208(1).)
fact.note: The research did not read the state-law section of the Mi'kmaq Nation Restoration Act that applies general state law (30 M.R.S. § 7204 returned 404), so the extent of residual state jurisdiction is not confirmed. Section 7208(1): "the Mi'kmaq Nation has the right to exercise exclusive jurisdiction, separate and distinct from the State, over" listed matters. Part 3 of the federal act (§ 6(b)) gives the Band and its lands "the same status as other tribes" under the 1980 act. Also cites: maine-revised-statutes-title-30-section-7208.

fact.detail: Settlement lands of the Narragansett Indian Tribe are subject to the civil and criminal laws and jurisdiction of Rhode Island; the First Circuit held this grant valid and covers civil regulatory jurisdiction. (Pub. L. No. 95-395, § 9, 92 Stat. at 817; Rhode Island v. Narragansett Indian Tribe, 19 F.3d 685, 694 (1st Cir. 1994).)
fact.note: Applies to "settlement lands"; the research did not research later trust acquisitions. The 1996 amendment (Pub. L. 104-208, § 330, 110 Stat. 3009-227) kept the sentence as § 9(a) and added § 9(b), settlement lands are not "Indian lands" for the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. 25 U.S.C. § 1708 is "omitted" from the Code. Whether Narragansett's "civil regulatory" reach holds today was not rechecked beyond the 1994 opinion. Also cites: rhode-island-v-narragansett-indian-tribe-1994, public-law-104-208-section-330.

fact.detail: Congress declared the Mashantucket Pequot reservation Indian country subject to Connecticut jurisdiction to the maximum extent provided in title IV of the 1968 Act (the Public Law 280 consent provisions), waiving the special-election requirement of § 406. (Pub. L. No. 98-134, § 6, 97 Stat. at 855.)
fact.note: The statute's sentence continues "to the maximum extent provided in title IV of such Act." 25 U.S.C. § 1755 is "omitted" from the Code. The text layer of this page prints "title the research V of s u c h Act" so the research stopped the quote earlier.

fact.detail: Congress consented to Connecticut's assumption of criminal jurisdiction over offenses by or against Indians on the Mohegan reservation, without waiving federal jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. § 1153 or ending the Tribe's concurrent jurisdiction. (Pub. L. No. 103-377, § 6, 108 Stat. at 3505.)
fact.note: Criminal only. Quote skips the words "Subject to subsection (b)," at the start of § 6(a). 25 U.S.C. § 1775d (omitted from the Code).

fact.detail: Settlement lands and other Indian-held land in the town of Gay Head (Aquinnah) are subject to the civil and criminal laws, ordinances and jurisdiction of Massachusetts and the town, except as the Act or the State Implementing Act expressly provides. (Pub. L. No. 100-95, § 9, 101 Stat. at 709.)
fact.note: Section 7(a) (101 Stat. at 707) also bars the tribal council from exercising jurisdiction "in contravention of" the Act and Massachusetts criminal and civil regulatory law. 25 U.S.C. § 1771g is "omitted" from the Code. The research did not research Aquinnah litigation after 1987. No comparable statute found for the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe.

fact.detail: South Carolina has civil, criminal and regulatory jurisdiction over the Catawba Tribe, its members and lands as over any other person or land, except where the State Act or federal implementing law says otherwise; federal law adopts the Settlement Agreement and State Act for these questions. (S.C. Code Ann. § 27-16-40; Pub. L. No. 103-116, § 10(1), 107 Stat. at 1126.)
fact.note: Federal side: § 10(1), "All matters involving tribal powers, immunities, and jurisdiction, whether criminal, civil, or regulatory, shall be governed by the terms and provisions of the Settlement Agreement and the State Act." Section 5(e)(?) of the federal Act (107 Stat. at 1122): the Act does not "deprive the State of jurisdiction other than as expressly provided." The State Act also lets the Tribe create tribal courts (S.C. Code Ann. §§ 27-16-110 to -120 not fully read). Also cites: public-law-103-116.

fact.detail: Texas exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction within the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo reservation as if it had assumed that jurisdiction with the tribe's consent under 25 U.S.C. §§ 1321 and 1322. (Pub. L. No. 100-89, § 105(f), 101 Stat. 666, 668.)
fact.note: 25 U.S.C. § 1300g-4 is "omitted" from the Code. Gaming provisions (§ 107) and Ysleta del Sur Pueblo v. Texas, 596 U.S. 685 (2022), were not analyzed.

fact.detail: Texas exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction within the Alabama-Coushatta reservation as if it had assumed that jurisdiction with the tribe's consent under 25 U.S.C. §§ 1321 and 1322. (Pub. L. No. 100-89, § 206(f), 101 Stat. at 671-72.)
fact.note: Quote sentence is identical to § 105(f); it appears at the bottom of 101 Stat. 671 and top of 672. Codified (as omitted) at 25 U.S.C. § 736.

fact.detail: Texas exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction over the Kickapoo band's trust lands in Maverick County as if it had assumed it under the 1968 Act, and may receive retrocession under § 403. (Pub. L. No. 97-429, § 6, 96 Stat. at 2270.)
fact.note: 25 U.S.C. § 1300b-15 is "omitted" from the Code. This statute was not on the research brief; found through the Cornell notes.

fact.detail: Florida's Public Law 280 assumption (Fla. Stat. § 285.16) continues in force on land taken into trust under the Seminole land claims settlement unless the United States accepts retrocession, and Florida alcohol, gambling and cigarette laws also apply there. (Pub. L. No. 100-228, § 6(d)(1), 101 Stat. at 1560.)
fact.note: Quote is the first part of the clause; it continues "shall continue in full force and effect on such lands unless the United States accepts a retrocession." 25 U.S.C. § 1772d is "omitted" from the Code. The Miccosukee Tribe and Poarch Band: no similar statute found (not researched in depth).

fact.detail: The 1980 restoration act directs Utah to exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over the Paiute reservation and persons on it as if Utah had assumed jurisdiction under Public Law 280, and under Utah Code §§ 63-36-9 to -21 (now Utah Code § 9-9-201 et seq.). (Pub. L. No. 96-227, § 7(b), 94 Stat. at 320.)
fact.note: The text refers to the Utah consent statute already recorded (special election). The research did not determine whether the tribe has voted; Pub. L. 109-126, § 4 (2005) amended the reservation provisions and was not read. Goldberg (2010) lists this under Utah as conferring state jurisdiction. 25 U.S.C. § 766 is "omitted" from the Code. Renumbering 63-36-9 to 9-9-201 is from your earlier reading, not mine.

fact.detail: The 1948 act that gave Iowa criminal jurisdiction over offenses by or against Indians on the Sac and Fox (Meskwaki) Reservation was repealed on Dec. 11, 2018. (Pub. L. No. 115-301, 132 Stat. 4395.)
fact.note: Original grant: Act of June 30, 1948, ch. 759, 62 Stat. 1161, "jurisdiction is hereby conferred on the State of Iowa over offenses committed by or against Indians on the Sac and Fox Indian Reservation in that State" (marginal headnotes interleave in the scan text layer). Iowa civil jurisdiction (Iowa Code § 1.12) was already recorded and is separate. Also cites: statutes-at-large-62-1161.

fact.detail: Mississippi has no Public Law 280 or special-act jurisdiction over Choctaw trust lands that the research found; the Supreme Court held that where the Major Crimes Act applies the State has no similar jurisdiction. (United States v. John, 437 U.S. 634, 653 (1978).)
fact.note: Narrow: John concerns a Major Crimes Act offense (assault with intent to kill) on Choctaw trust land. "Not assumed" for broader civil or criminal matters rests on not finding any grant; the research did not find a Mississippi statute assuming jurisdiction. Quote begins mid-sentence in the opinion.

(1955 Nev. Stat. ch. 198, §§ 1-3, at 297.)
fact.note: Mapped to the nations whose lands appear in the 1975 and 1988 retrocession notices (see those facts). Odger's Ranch and Ruby Valley Allotment, named in the 1975 notice, are not mapped because the research could not tie them to a roster entry. The 1955 act was later folded into NRS 41.430 (history line "1:198:1955"). Also cites: davis-v-warden-1972.

fact.detail: Since July 1, 1974 NRS 41.430 applies only where the tribe consented, by referendum under sections 6-14 of the 1973 act or under 25 U.S.C. § 1326; where a tribe refused, Nevada "recedes from and relinquishes" jurisdiction. The Indian affairs commission was to hold the referenda by June 4, 1974. (1973 Nev. Stat. ch. 601, §§ 1, 6, at 1051-53; Nev. Rev. Stat. § 41.430(3)-(4).)
fact.note: Sections 1-5 took effect July 1, 1974 (§ 16). The current NRS text still carries this language. Goldberg (2010) says no tribe asked to continue; the 1976 AIPRC report says Ely Colony alone chose to keep state jurisdiction. Goldberg's date for the assumption (1967) conflicts with the Statutes (1955). Also cites: nevada-revised-statutes-41-430.

fact.detail: The Pyramid Lake Reservation was never under Nevada jurisdiction under the 1955 act: Washoe County petitioned and the Governor excluded it by proclamation of June 27, 1955, and the exclusion was never withdrawn. (Davis v. Warden, 88 Nev. 443, 446, 498 P.2d 1346 (1972).)
fact.note: The court held state courts lacked jurisdiction over Pyramid Lake members' crimes on the reservation and vacated the convictions. Nevada Supreme Court, 1972.

fact.detail: The 1975 retrocession notice lists only the areas over which Nevada had acquired jurisdiction; Fallon, Walker River, Duck Valley, Fort McDermitt, Moapa, Las Vegas, Summit Lake, Yerington, Fort Mojave and Timbisha lands are not on it, and the notice does not say why. (40 Fed. Reg. 27,501.)
fact.note: INFERENCE, not stated in any source the research read: because the notice covers only jurisdiction "acquired by the State," a nation absent from it was not under state jurisdiction in 1975. The 1976 AIPRC report (fn. 21) lists the previously covered areas and omits these nations. The 1955 act let counties exclude Indian country by Governor's proclamation (Pyramid Lake did); the research did not locate the proclamations or minutes for the other counties, so the reason for each nation is unconfirmed. Fort Mojave also has AZ/CA lands; Duck Valley ID; Fort McDermitt OR. Also cites: american-indian-policy-review-commission-task-force-four-1976, goldberg-2010-tribal-jurisdictional-status-analysis.
